messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: need help with Wishart
parts:
I'm totally baffled by our Wishart and after two days
am finally out of ideas on how to approach debugging
it. I'll need help from someone who's better at matrices
than me to figure this out.

We only tested the round-trip behavior of the transform,
not its derivatives. So Ben's hypothesis that it might
be a problem with the Jacobian in the transform is still
a possibility.

A big problem for me is that I have no clue what the bits of
Ben's transform code mean.

We've checked the definitions of the Wishart a gazillion
times and they pass all our unit tests checking against
MCMCpack.

I could just add 2 to the DOF and everything works the
way it should, which is really really puzzling.

I'm beginning to wonder if everyone copied the
wrong form of the density from each other. It's
a long shot, but here's my reasoning.

There's a term in the log probability

lp += multiply_log(0.5 * (nu - k - 1.0), determinant(W));

where

multiply_log(x,y) == x * log(y);

BDA, Bishop's machine learning book, and the Wikipedia
all agree on the sign of 1 in this term.
And the results using this definition agree with MCMCpack, which
is how we generated unit tests.

Furthermore, everyone agrees the expectation is the dof
times the scale matrix. But our posterior mean is
(dof - 2) * scale matrix.

There's a serious right skew to the posterior, but
I can't believe it's just a failure to sample outliers
as the results so consistently match what we should get
with two fewer degrees of freedom.

So what if instead of (nu - k - 1), the term were
(nu - (k - 1))?

It gives us right answer from sampling. It effectively
adds 2 to the degrees of freedom, and previously it
was behaving as if the dof were 2 less than specified,
so getting the right posterior mean with this hack
in itself isn't surprising.

The suggested term (nu - (k - 1)) has the property that
nu = k - 1 is the value at which the term changes sign,
but that seems irrelevant given we're on the log scale.
Also, (nu - (k - 1)) is the smallest term inside the
product of Gamma functions.

Help?

- Bob

Here is something to consider. If we try a 2x2 example, we can avoid
all that LKJ transformation stuff. Like this

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan-svn$ cat /tmp/wishart2x2.stan
transformed data {
cov_matrix(2) S;

for (i in 1:2)
for (j in 1:2)
S[i,j] <- 0.0;

S[1,1] <- 2.0;
S[2,2] <- 0.5;
}
parameters {
double(-1,1) rho;
double(0,) var1;
double(0,) var2;
}
model {
double cov;
matrix(2,2) W;

W[1,1] <- var1;
W[2,2] <- var2;

cov <- rho * sqrt(var1 * var2);
W[1,2] <- cov;
W[2,1] <- cov;
W ~ wishart(4, S);
}

So, implicitly we have improper uniform priors over the positive reals
on the two variance parameters and uniform on (-1,1) for the
correlation. Compile and run ...

Yes, we do need a Jacobian for that change of variables (and I thought
it was already being done), but it should be really simple. The
Jacobian matrix, J, should be diagonal and the diagonal elements are
just the partial derivatives of whatever transformation stan is doing
to enforce the bounds. And the determinant of that diagonal Jacobian
is just the product of its diagonal entries, or the log determinant is
the sum of the logs of the diagonal entries.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: need help with Wishart
parts:
Good news. The Jacobian is indeed very
simple (I really do need the practice), because
indeed it's a triangular matrix where two of the
diagonal entries are 1. The Jacobian is

sqrt(var1 * var2)

and when I plug the log of that in I get
the right answer from Stan. With my newfound
R tricks, we have (I used a dof=5):

> as.matrix(colMeans(read.csv("samples.csv")))
[,1]
rho 0.01113324
var1 9.86215400
var2 2.47388116

I checked the model in with the addition of the
Jacobian as wishart2x2.stan in basic_distributions.
Here it is:

stan/models/basic_distributions/wishart2x2.stan
------------------
transformed data {
cov_matrix(2) S;

S[1,1] <- 2.0;
S[2,2] <- 0.5;
}
parameters {
double(-1,1) rho;
double(0,) var1;
double(0,) var2;
}
model {
double cov;
matrix(2,2) W;
cov <- rho * sqrt(var1 * var2);

W ~ wishart(5, S);
}

Now I'll try the same model with the
transforms and see what happens. Stay tuned.

- Bob
